LLM_description:
Subject: Service Center Staffing Review and Cost-Minimizing Assignment

Context
We operate a multi-station service center that includes help desks, transaction counters, and specialized departments. Each station receives customers at a known hourly pace, and each interaction takes a predictable amount of time on average. Our staffing pool includes several types of team members with different skills, hourly costs, and service speeds. The combination of varying customer volumes, different handling speeds by station, and qualification limits creates a complex assignment problem.

Situation
- Customer arrivals are forecasted by station in customers per hour. Demand patterns are stable enough for planning purposes but differ across stations.
- Handling speed is represented as average minutes per customer and varies by staff type and station. Some staff types are not qualified to serve at certain stations.
- Each staff type carries a distinct hourly labor cost and has a limited number of available personnel.
- There are many potential station–staff assignments, but a subset is not permissible due to qualifications. Choosing an effective mix cannot be done reliably by manual judgment alone.

Challenge
We must decide how many people of each staff type to assign to each station so that:
- Every station has adequate coverage throughout the planning period.
- Combined processing capability at each station comfortably keeps pace with incoming customers.
- Staff are used efficiently but not pushed so hard that service quality degrades or breaks occur.
- We stay within the available headcount for each staff type.
- We control total hourly staffing cost.

Service Quality and Coverage Requirements
- Capacity headroom: Arrivals are measured per hour while handling time is measured in minutes per customer. This means we need to align hourly demand with per-customer processing time. Practically, the group of staff assigned to a station must, together, be able to process more customers per hour than we expect to arrive. This headroom is intentional. It ensures staff are not scheduled at full tilt and that short spikes, breaks, and variability can be absorbed without excessive queues.
- Utilization policy: We have a management policy that staff should not be occupied more than a target fraction of their time at a station. This limits how heavily each station can be loaded and reinforces the capacity buffer noted above.
- Minimum coverage: Each station requires a minimum number of staff to maintain safety, continuity, and service presence even during lulls, training, or short absences.
- Qualifications: Staff may only be assigned to stations where they are trained and authorized to serve. Some combinations are not allowed.
- Availability: The number of people of each staff type is limited. Assignments must not exceed what is available to work in the period.
- Cost discipline: Staff types have different hourly rates. We should prefer lower-cost resources where they are qualified and provide sufficient speed, while using higher-cost specialists where they are uniquely capable or faster enough to justify the expense.

Goal
Assign staff types to stations in a way that meets service demand and coverage requirements, observes qualification and availability limits, respects the utilization policy, and minimizes total hourly staffing cost. The desired outcome is a clear, defensible staffing mix by station that delivers predictable service levels at the lowest sustainable labor spend.

Next Steps
- Validate station demand and confirm that arrival rates reflect the planning horizon.
- Confirm handling times by staff type and station and identify all non-qualified combinations.
- Reaffirm the target utilization standard and minimum coverage levels by station.
- Build the staffing assignment using the validated data, evaluate the resulting service headroom at each station, and compare total hourly cost against alternatives.
- Review the proposed plan with station leads and HR to ensure feasibility and alignment with training and labor policies.

LLM_description_template:
Subject: Service Center Staffing Review and Cost-Minimizing Assignment

Context
We operate a multi-station service center that includes help desks, transaction counters, and specialized departments. Each station receives customers at a known hourly pace, and each interaction takes a predictable amount of time on average. Our staffing pool includes several types of team members with different skills, hourly costs, and service speeds. The combination of varying customer volumes, different handling speeds by station, and qualification limits creates a complex assignment problem.

Situation
- Customer arrivals are forecasted by station in customers per hour. Demand patterns are stable enough for planning purposes but differ across stations.
- Handling speed is represented as average minutes per customer and varies by staff type and station. Some staff types are not qualified to serve at certain stations.
- Each staff type carries a distinct hourly labor cost and has a limited number of available personnel.
- There are many potential station–staff assignments, but a subset is not permissible due to qualifications. Choosing an effective mix cannot be done reliably by manual judgment alone.

Challenge
We must decide how many people of each staff type to assign to each station so that:
- Every station has adequate coverage throughout the planning period.
- Combined processing capability at each station comfortably keeps pace with incoming customers.
- Staff are used efficiently but not pushed so hard that service quality degrades or breaks occur.
- We stay within the available headcount for each staff type.
- We control total hourly staffing cost.

Service Quality and Coverage Requirements
- Capacity headroom: Arrivals are measured per hour while handling time is measured in minutes per customer. This means we need to align hourly demand with per-customer processing time. Practically, the group of staff assigned to a station must, together, be able to process more customers per hour than we expect to arrive. This headroom is intentional. It ensures staff are not scheduled at full tilt and that short spikes, breaks, and variability can be absorbed without excessive queues.
- Utilization policy: We have a management policy that staff should not be occupied more than a target fraction of their time at a station. This limits how heavily each station can be loaded and reinforces the capacity buffer noted above.
- Minimum coverage: Each station requires a minimum number of staff to maintain safety, continuity, and service presence even during lulls, training, or short absences.
- Qualifications: Staff may only be assigned to stations where they are trained and authorized to serve. Some combinations are not allowed.
- Availability: The number of people of each staff type is limited. Assignments must not exceed what is available to work in the period.
- Cost discipline: Staff types have different hourly rates. We should prefer lower-cost resources where they are qualified and provide sufficient speed, while using higher-cost specialists where they are uniquely capable or faster enough to justify the expense.

Goal
Assign staff types to stations in a way that meets service demand and coverage requirements, observes qualification and availability limits, respects the utilization policy, and minimizes total hourly staffing cost. The desired outcome is a clear, defensible staffing mix by station that delivers predictable service levels at the lowest sustainable labor spend.

Next Steps
- Validate station demand and confirm that arrival rates reflect the planning horizon.
- Confirm handling times by staff type and station and identify all non-qualified combinations.
- Reaffirm the target utilization standard and minimum coverage levels by station.
- Build the staffing assignment using the validated data, evaluate the resulting service headroom at each station, and compare total hourly cost against alternatives.
- Review the proposed plan with station leads and HR to ensure feasibility and alignment with training and labor policies.
